public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 318

*References:*
  - [erdosproblems.com/318](https://www.erdosproblems.com/318)
  - [ErSt75] Erdős, P. and Straus, E. G., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 183.
  - [Sa75] Sattler, R., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 184-189.
  - [Sa82b] Sattler, R., On Erdős property P₁ for the arithmetical sequence. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch.
    Indag. Math. (1982), 347--352.
  - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
    theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
  - [La26] D. Larsen, [Erdős problem 318](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/blob/main/318.pdf) (2026)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Set Real

namespace Erdos318

/-- A set `A : Set ℕ` is said to have property `P₁` if for any nonconstant sequence
`f : A → {-1, 1}`, one can always select a finite, nonempty subset `S ⊆ A \ {0}` such that
`∑ n ∈ S, fₙ / n = 0`. This is defined in [Sa82b]. -/
def P₁ (A : Set ℕ) : Prop := ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
  f ∘ (Subtype.val : (A \ {0} : Set ℕ) → ℕ) ≠ (fun _ => 1) →
  f ∘ (Subtype.val : (A \ {0} : Set ℕ) → ℕ) ≠ (fun _ => - 1) →
  Set.range f ⊆ {1, -1} →
  ∃ S : Finset ℕ, S.Nonempty ∧ ↑S ⊆ A \ {0} ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, f n / n = 0

/-- `ℕ` has property `P₁`. This is proved in [ErSt75]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos318.lean#L761"]
theorem erdos_318.variants.univ : P₁ univ := by
  sorry

/-- Sattler proved in [Sa75] that the set of odd numbers has property `P₁`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos318.lean#L782"]
theorem erdos_318.variants.odd : P₁ {n | Odd n} := by
  sorry

/-- The set of squares does not have property `P₁`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.squares : ¬ P₁ ({n | IsSquare n}) := by
  simp only [P₁, not_forall, not_exists, not_and]
  -- Consider the function `f` that sends `1` to `1` and sends all other numbers to `-1`.
  refine ⟨fun n => if n = 1 then 1 else - 1, fun h => ?_, fun h => ?_,
    fun x ⟨y, hy⟩ => ?_, fun S h hs => ?_⟩
  · have : (- 1 : ℝ) = 1 := by simpa using congr_fun h ⟨4, ⟨⟨2, by grind⟩, by grind⟩⟩
    grind
  · have : 1 = (- 1 : ℝ) := by simpa using congr_fun h ⟨1, ⟨IsSquare.one, by grind⟩⟩
    grind
  · by_cases x = 1 <;> grind
  -- Consider two cases: `1 ∈ S` or `1 ∉ S`. In the first case, the finite sum over `S` is bounded
  -- below by `1 - (π ^ 2 / 6 - 1)`, which is positive. In the second case, the finite sum over `S`
  -- is negative.
  by_cases h1 : 1 ∈ S
  · rw [Finset.sum_eq_add_sum_sdiff_singleton 1 _ (by simp [h1]), Finset.sum_congr rfl
      (g := fun n : ℕ => (- 1 : ℝ) / n)]
    · simp only [↓reduceIte, Nat.cast_one, div_self one_ne_zero, ← ne_eq, div_eq_mul_one_div
        (- 1 : ℝ), ← Finset.mul_sum, neg_one_mul (∑ x ∈ S \ {1}, 1 / (x : ℝ)), ← sub_eq_add_neg]
      apply ne_of_gt
      calc
      _ < 1 - (π ^ 2 / 6 - 1) := by
        have : π ^ 2 < 3.15 ^ 2 := by gcongr; exact Real.pi_lt_d2
        linarith
      _ = 1 - (∑' n : ℕ, 1 / (n : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1) := by congr; exact hasSum_zeta_two.tsum_eq.symm
      _ ≤ 1 - ∑ n ∈ S \ {1}, 1 / (n : ℝ) := by
        gcongr
        have : 1 = 1 / ((1 : ℕ) : ℝ) := by norm_cast; grind
        nth_rewrite 3 [this]
        rw [le_sub_iff_add_le, ← Finset.sum_eq_sum_sdiff_singleton_add h1]
        let S' := S.preimage (· ^ 2) (Function.Injective.injOn
          (Nat.pow_left_injective (by decide)))
        have hS' : S'.map ⟨(· ^ 2), Nat.pow_left_injective (by decide)⟩ = S := by
          apply Finset.coe_injective
          have h : (S : Set ℕ) ⊆ Set.range (· ^ 2) :=
            hs.trans (by simp [isSquare_iff_exists_sq, Set.subset_def])
          simpa [S', Set.image_preimage_eq_iff] using h
        rw [← hS', Finset.sum_map, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk]
        simpa [Nat.cast_pow] using Summable.sum_le_tsum S' (fun _ _ => by positivity) (by simp)
    · intro _ _; grind
  · suffices ∑ n ∈ S, (fun n ↦ if n = 1 then 1 else - 1) n / (n : ℝ) < 0 from by linarith
    refine Finset.sum_neg (fun p hp => ?_) h
    have : p ≠ 1 := by grind
    simp_all [neg_div, zero_lt_iff, (not_iff_not.2 mem_singleton_iff).1 (hs hp).2]

/-- For any infinite set `A` containing exactly one positive even number, `A` does not have
property `P₁`. Sattler [Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős, who presumably found this after
[ErGr80]. The element `0` is not counted, since `P₁` ignores it, and the infinitude hypothesis
excludes degenerate sets such as `{2}`, on which `P₁` holds vacuously. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.Infinite)
    (hA' : {n | n ∈ A \ {0} ∧ Even n}.ncard = 1) : ¬ P₁ A := by
  sorry

/-- There exists a set `A` with positive density that does not have property `P₁`.
#TODO: prove this lemma by assuming `erdos_318.contain_single_even`.

The density sits in an existential, so `HasPosDensity` is the *stronger* reading here and
weakening it to positive lower density would claim less, which is the opposite of the usual
situation for Erdős' "positive density". It also costs nothing: by
`erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even` a witness only needs exactly one even element, and the
odd numbers together with one even number have density `1 / 2` on the nose. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.parts.i : ∃ A : Set ℕ, HasPosDensity A ∧ ¬ P₁ A := by
  sorry

/-- Every infinite arithmetic progression has property `P₁`. This is proved in [Sa82b]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos318.lean#L599"]
theorem erdos_318.variants.infinite_AP {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.IsAPOfLength ⊤) : P₁ A := by
  sorry

/--
Does the set of squares excluding 1 have property `P₁`?

Larsen [La26] proved that this set does have property `P₁`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.parts.ii : answer(True) ↔  P₁ ({n | IsSquare n} \ {1}) := by
  sorry

end Erdos318

findings.description: Reference slip. The docstring says "Sattler [Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős", but the module docstring's reference list has no [Sa82]. It lists only [Sa75] and [Sa82b]. erdosproblems.com treats [Sa82] and [Sa82b] as two different papers: Erdős is credited in [Sa82], and the AP theorem is in [Sa82b]. As written, a reader cannot resolve the citation. The mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/318 (Wayback snapshot 2026-09-04): "(Sattler [Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős, who presumably found this after [ErGr80].) Sattler [Sa82b] proved the answer to the original question is yes ... Sattler also announced a proof of the final question ... in [Sa82] and [Sa82b]". Crossref lists two Sattler papers in the same 1982 Indag. Math. issue: 'On Erdös property P1 for the sequence of squarefree numbers' (pp. 341-346, DOI 10.1016/1385-7258(82)90025-7) and 'On Erdös property P1 for the arithmetical sequence' (pp. 347-352).
findings.suggested_fix: Add a [Sa82] entry to the module docstring's reference list. It is presumably R. Sattler, 'On Erdős property P₁ for the sequence of squarefree numbers', Indag. Math. 44 (1982), 341–346; confirm against the erdosproblems.com bibliography.

findings.description: The docstring says the property is about "any nonconstant sequence `f : A → {-1, 1}`". The Lean definition only asks that f be non-constant on `A \ {0}`: the hypotheses are `f ∘ Subtype.val ≠ fun _ => 1` and `≠ fun _ => -1` on `↥(A \ {0})`. The two readings differ whenever 0 ∈ A, which happens for `univ`, `{n | IsSquare n}`, `{n | IsSquare n} \ {1}` and APs starting at 0. For example, with A = ℕ, take f(0) = 1 and f = -1 elsewhere. This f is non-constant on A, but no zero sum exists. I proved in Lean that the literal-docstring variant (non-constancy on all of A) fails for `Set.univ`. The Lean `P₁ univ` is the Erdős–Straus theorem. The Lean definition is the correct one; only the docstring is imprecise.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/318: "Let A ⊆ ℕ ... and f : A → {-1,1} be a non-constant function". Here A is a set of positive integers, so 0 never occurs. In Lean's ℕ, the element 0 must be discarded from the non-constancy condition too, as the Lean code does.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword the docstring, e.g. "... if for any `f : A \ {0} → {-1, 1}` that is not constant, one can select a finite nonempty `S ⊆ A \ {0}` with `∑ n ∈ S, f n / n = 0` (the element 0 is ignored throughout)."

reformulations.difference: Larsen's Theorem 6, the cited proof, is a partition statement: any partition of the squares > 1 into two non-empty parts X, Y has non-empty finite X' ⊆ X, Y' ⊆ Y with ∑_{X'} 1/n = ∑_{Y'} 1/n. The Lean instead states `P₁ ({n | IsSquare n} \ {1})`, using erdosproblems.com's ±1-signing form, and the set still contains 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: P₁ only looks at A \ {0}, both in the non-constancy hypothesis and in S ⊆ A \ {0}. So the relevant set is exactly the squares ≥ 4. In a scratch file I proved `P₁ A ↔ PartitionForm A` for every `A : Set ℕ`, where PartitionForm is Larsen's formulation. Forward: from X build f = 1 on X and -1 off X. A zero-sum S splits into S ∩ X and S \ X, and both are non-empty because every term is non-zero and has a fixed sign in each part. Backward: set X = {f = 1} and S = X' ∪ Y'. With `answer(True)` the statement is exactly Larsen's theorem, which erdosproblems.com records as settling the third question 'yes'.

reformulations.difference: The source asks a yes/no question: "What about if A is an arbitrary set of positive density?". The Lean does not use `answer(False) ↔ ∀ A, A.HasPosDensity → P₁ A`. It states the negative answer directly as a counterexample, `∃ A, A.HasPosDensity ∧ ¬ P₁ A`, with positive natural density.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Classically, ¬(∀ A, H A → P₁ A) ↔ ∃ A, H A ∧ ¬P₁ A. In an existential, natural density (which must exist) is the strongest reading of "positive density". The source's remark gives such a witness: a set with exactly one even number. The odd numbers together with {2} have density exactly 1/2. So the statement is the source's negative answer, and it is true.

reformulations.difference: `A.IsAPOfLength ⊤` allows an AP of naturals with first term 0, i.e. {0, d, 2d, ...}. The source only considers APs of positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `IsAPOfLength ⊤` means A = {a + n·d : n ∈ ℕ} with A infinite, which forces d ≥ 1. If a = 0, then A \ {0} = {d, 2d, ...}, which is itself an infinite AP of positive integers with first term d. P₁ only sees A \ {0}, so the Lean statement is equivalent to 'every infinite AP of positive integers has P₁'. That is what erdosproblems.com attributes to Sattler [Sa82b]: "any arithmetic progression has this property".

reformulations.difference: f is a real-valued function on all of ℕ with range ⊆ {1, -1}. Non-constancy is written as 'f on A \ {0} is neither constantly 1 nor constantly -1'. The element 0 is ignored throughout.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Any f : A → {±1} extends to all of ℕ, and values outside A \ {0} never enter the sum. On a non-empty domain, a {±1}-valued function is non-constant iff it is neither constantly 1 nor constantly -1. When A \ {0} is empty or a singleton, both readings are vacuous (checked in Lean for ∅). The sum divides only by n ∈ S ⊆ A \ {0}, so `x / 0` is never reached. For sets of positive integers this is exactly the source's property.

review.notes:
No misformalization found. I compared every declaration with erdosproblems.com/318 (snapshot of 2026-09-04) and its three questions:
- Question 1 (infinite APs, answer yes, Sattler [Sa82b]) is `variants.infinite_AP`.
- Question 2 (arbitrary sets of positive density, answer no) is `parts.i`.
- Question 3 (squares excluding 1, answer yes, Larsen) is `parts.ii` with `answer(True)`.
- The source's remarks are `variants.univ` (ErSt75), `variants.odd` (Sa75), `variants.squares` (1 must be excluded) and `variants.contain_single_even` (Erdős's one-even-number observation).
All categories are `research solved` (`squares` is `test`), which matches the source's SOLVED status. There are no status issues.

Lean checks (all in /workspace/review, all compile):
- `#print` confirms `P₁` elaborates with `∑ n ∈ S, f n / ↑n` and non-constancy on `↥(A \ {0})`.
- `P₁ ∅` holds vacuously.
- The hypotheses of `contain_single_even` are satisfiable: odd numbers ∪ {2} is infinite and has exactly one positive even element.
- `univ` and 3ℕ satisfy `IsAPOfLength ⊤`.
- `P₁ A ↔` Larsen's partition form, for all A.
- The literal-docstring variant of `P₁` fails for `univ`.
- `variants.squares` is fully proved: `#print axioms` shows no `sorryAx`.

`contain_single_even` needs its `A.Infinite` hypothesis, and it correctly leaves 0 out of the even count. The source's literal remark fails for degenerate sets such as {2}, where P₁ holds vacuously. The plby proof file records that an earlier FC version without this hypothesis was false; the current statement is repaired and true.

The `formal_proof` links (L599, L761, L782) point at theorems with the same statement, using identical `P₁` and `IsAPOfLength` definitions. The same plby file also proves `parts.i` (`not_erdos_318`, L385), which is not linked. Its `HasPosDensity` comes from a local `Util.Density`, which I did not compare with FC's.

Two trivial docstring issues, not raised as findings:
- The `parts.i` docstring's #TODO names `erdos_318.contain_single_even`; the declaration is `erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even`.
- The first question is named `variants.infinite_AP` rather than a `parts` entry.

I could not read the ErGr80 book (p.42) or Sattler's 1982 papers: ScienceDirect blocks automated access and the Wayback Machine was refusing connections. For their content I relied on erdosproblems.com's summary. The plby formal proof of `infinite_AP` backs up the claim that it holds for every infinite AP.
